question: How much deposit should I pay a flooring contractor?
title: How Much Deposit Should You Pay a Flooring Contractor?
h1: How Much Should You Pay Upfront for a Flooring Job?
description: A flooring contractor deposit typically runs 10-25% of the job, tied to milestones, not paid in full upfront, according to Angi's 2026 guidance.
capsule: A typical flooring contractor deposit runs 10% to 25% of the total job, sometimes up to 50% on smaller jobs where material has to be special-ordered. The rest should be tied to milestones like material delivery, demo completion and finished install, never paid in full before work has started, according to Angi's contractor payment guidance.

sections.h2: How Much Deposit Is Normal for a Flooring Job?
sections.html:
Angi's guidance on contractor payments puts a typical deposit at 10-25% of the total project cost, with smaller jobs sometimes running higher, up to 10-50%, because a small job still has fixed costs like ordering material. What shouldn't happen on any size job is paying the full amount before work starts. Payments should track progress: a deposit to begin, then draws tied to material delivery, demo, and completed installation.

Think of it in dollar terms on a mid-size job. On a $6,000 vinyl plank install, a 10-25% deposit lands somewhere around $600-$1,500, with the balance due as the work actually happens rather than all at once on day one. A $2,000 bathroom tile job might run a higher percentage deposit simply because the fixed costs, tile, thinset, waterproofing membrane, are a bigger share of a smaller total.

sections.h2: Why Contractors Ask for Money Upfront
sections.html:
The deposit usually covers material ordering, not labor. Vinyl plank and standard tile ship fast, but wide-plank European oak, herringbone patterns, or a specific SPC color can carry longer lead times, and a contractor doesn't want to carry that material cost personally before a customer has committed. A deposit tied to material, with the rest due as work progresses, is a normal and reasonable structure.

It also protects the homeowner in a roundabout way. A contractor who won't start ordering material without some commitment from you is, in practice, a contractor who isn't stockpiling unsold inventory or juggling five other jobs' material on your dime. The deposit structure itself is a small signal about how the business runs.

Be cautious of a contractor who wants full payment before any material has been ordered or any work has started, who only accepts cash with no receipt, or who won't put the payment schedule in the written quote alongside the scope of work. A legitimate flooring contractor has no reason to avoid putting payment terms in writing next to the job description.

Pressure to decide and pay on the spot, during the same visit as the estimate, is another thing worth slowing down for. A reasonable timeline includes time to read the written quote, ask questions, and compare it against another bid if you want one. None of that should feel rushed, and a contractor confident in their pricing generally isn't the one pushing you to sign immediately. Take the quote home, sleep on it if you want to, and call with questions before you commit anything. A contractor worth hiring will still be there in a week, and the job will still get scheduled once you're ready.

We build the payment schedule into the same written, line-itemized quote as the scope of work, so material, labor and payment milestones are all in one document you can review before signing. If you want specifics for your project size and material selection, ask us during your free estimate; we'll walk through the schedule before any deposit changes hands.

For more on what should be in a flooring quote generally, see our guide on questions to ask before hiring or browse financing options if you'd rather spread the total cost instead of a large upfront payment. Either way, you should walk away from the estimate with a document that spells out dollar amounts and timing, not a verbal understanding you have to remember weeks later.

faqs.q: Is it normal to pay 50% upfront on a small flooring job?
faqs.a: It can be, particularly on jobs under a few thousand dollars where material has to be special-ordered. What matters more than the percentage is that the remaining balance is tied to milestones, not paid all at once before work begins.

faqs.q: What if a contractor asks for full payment before starting?
faqs.a: That's worth questioning. A reasonable payment structure ties draws to progress, deposit, material delivery, completed install, so you're never fully paid out before the work matches it.

faqs.q: Can I pay a flooring contractor with financing instead of a large deposit?
faqs.a: Many contractors, including us, offer financing that spreads the total cost instead of requiring a large cash deposit upfront. Ask about financing options during your estimate if that fits your situation better.
